measures: The fraction of predictions that exactly match the gold label.
strengths: Simple to compute and explain
Works for binary and multiclass problems
weaknesses: Misleading on imbalanced data: always predicting the majority class can score highly
Treats all errors as equally costly
use_when: Classes are roughly balanced and every type of error costs about the same.
avoid_when: One class dominates, for example fraud or toxicity detection, where a trivial classifier looks strong.

measures: Of the items predicted as positive, the fraction that are actually positive.
strengths: Directly reflects the cost of false positives
Can be computed per class
weaknesses: Can be inflated by predicting positive only rarely
Ignores false negatives entirely
use_when: False positives are expensive, as in spam filtering where flagging a real email is costly.
avoid_when: It is reported without recall, since a model that rarely predicts positive can reach near-perfect precision.

measures: Of the truly positive items, the fraction the model correctly identifies.
strengths: Directly reflects the cost of missed positives
Can be computed per class
weaknesses: Trivially maximised by predicting everything as positive
Ignores false positives entirely
use_when: Missing a positive is expensive, as in medical triage or safety screening.
avoid_when: It is reported without precision, since predicting every item as positive gives a recall of 1.

measures: The harmonic mean of precision and recall, averaged across classes: equally per class (macro), over all individual decisions (micro), or by class frequency (weighted).
strengths: Balances precision and recall in one number
Macro-F1 exposes poor performance on rare classes
weaknesses: Choice of averaging changes results a lot and is often not reported
Ignores true negatives
Does not use the classification threshold or the model's confidence
use_when: Classes are imbalanced and you need one number that accounts for both false positives and false negatives.
avoid_when: Results using different averaging modes are compared, or the true-negative rate matters.

measures: The correlation between predicted and true labels, computed from all four cells of the confusion matrix.
range_and_direction: -1 to 1; higher is better, 0 means no better than random.
strengths: Robust to class imbalance
Uses true negatives, unlike F1
weaknesses: Less intuitive to explain than accuracy or F1
Undefined when a row or column of the confusion matrix is all zeros (libraries usually return 0)
use_when: You want one balanced score for imbalanced binary classification, as in the GLUE CoLA task.
avoid_when: Stakeholders need a directly interpretable rate, such as 'what fraction of flagged items are real'.

measures: The probability that the model gives a randomly chosen positive a higher score than a randomly chosen negative, across all thresholds.
range_and_direction: 0 to 1; higher is better, 0.5 means random ranking.
strengths: Does not depend on a classification threshold
Evaluates the model's scores rather than its hard labels
weaknesses: Can look optimistic on heavily imbalanced data, where PR-AUC is more informative
Says nothing about calibration or the right operating threshold
use_when: You want to compare how well models rank examples before choosing a decision threshold.
avoid_when: Positives are very rare and you care about precision at the top, which PR-AUC captures better.

measures: Precision, recall and F1 over whole entity spans: a predicted entity counts only if its boundaries and type both match the gold entity exactly.
strengths: Matches the CoNLL-2003 standard evaluation
Penalises broken spans that token-level accuracy hides
weaknesses: No partial credit for nearly correct boundaries
Results depend on the tagging scheme (IOB1, IOB2, BIOES) and strict vs. lenient mode
use_when: You evaluate NER or other span-tagging tasks and want numbers comparable to published results.
avoid_when: Partially correct boundaries are acceptable in your application, since strict matching will understate quality.

measures: The fraction of predictions that exactly equal a gold answer after normalisation (lower-casing and removing punctuation and articles).
range_and_direction: 0 to 1 (SQuAD reports 0 to 100); higher is better.
strengths: Strict and unambiguous
Standard for SQuAD-style benchmarks
weaknesses: No credit for correct answers with extra or missing words
Unsuitable for free-form generated answers
use_when: Answers are short spans copied from a passage, as in SQuAD.
avoid_when: An LLM writes answers in its own words, so correct answers rarely match character for character.

measures: The F1 of word overlap between the predicted and gold answer, taking the best score across gold answers.
range_and_direction: 0 to 1 (SQuAD reports 0 to 100); higher is better.
strengths: Gives partial credit when Exact Match gives none
Standard alongside Exact Match
weaknesses: Rewards word overlap even when the answer is wrong
Penalises correct paraphrases
use_when: You evaluate span-extraction QA and want a softer companion to Exact Match.
avoid_when: Answers are long or abstractive, where word overlap tracks correctness poorly.

measures: The geometric mean of modified n-gram precisions (usually n = 1 to 4) against reference texts, multiplied by a brevity penalty for short outputs.
range_and_direction: 0 to 100 in sacreBLEU (0 to 1 in some libraries); higher is better.
strengths: Cheap, fast and fully reproducible with sacreBLEU
Decades of comparable results
weaknesses: Weak correlation with human judgement at the sentence level
Penalises valid paraphrases and synonyms
Scores change with tokenisation unless you use sacreBLEU
use_when: You compare MT systems on a corpus with fixed references and need results comparable to the literature.
avoid_when: You score single sentences, compare very different system types, or evaluate LLM output that rephrases freely.

measures: A character n-gram F-score against the reference, weighting recall more than precision (beta = 2); chrF++ also adds word unigrams and bigrams.
strengths: Correlates with human judgement better than BLEU in WMT studies
Handles morphologically rich languages well
Does not depend on word tokenisation
weaknesses: Still a surface-overlap metric that misses meaning-preserving paraphrases
Less widely reported than BLEU in older work
use_when: You need a cheap MT metric, especially for languages with rich morphology or no clear word boundaries.
avoid_when: You need to judge meaning preservation rather than surface similarity.

measures: The minimum number of edits (insertions, deletions, substitutions and phrase shifts) needed to turn the output into the reference, divided by the reference length.
range_and_direction: 0 and up (can exceed 100%); lower is better.
strengths: Easy to interpret as the post-editing effort required
Allows phrase shifts, unlike plain edit distance
weaknesses: Penalises valid alternative translations
Unbounded above, so scores for very bad outputs are hard to read
use_when: You estimate how much human post-editing translations will need.
avoid_when: Many different translations are valid and you have only one reference.

measures: A recall-weighted harmonic mean of unigram precision and recall, matching exact words, stems and WordNet synonyms, with a penalty for fragmented word order.
strengths: Gives credit for synonyms and stems
Correlates with human judgement better than BLEU at the sentence level
weaknesses: Synonym matching mostly depends on English WordNet
Slower than BLEU and less standard in recent work
use_when: You evaluate English generation and want some credit for synonyms without running a neural model.
avoid_when: You evaluate languages without good WordNet coverage.

measures: A quality score predicted by a multilingual neural model trained on human judgements, using the source sentence, the translation and (optionally) a reference.
range_and_direction: Depends on the model version: COMET-22 is roughly 0 to 1, older models can go negative; higher is better.
strengths: Among the best-correlated MT metrics in WMT metric shared tasks
Uses the source sentence, so it can detect translations that change the meaning
Reference-free versions (CometKiwi) can estimate quality without references
weaknesses: Scores are not comparable across COMET model versions
Needs a GPU for large test sets
Can miss specific errors such as wrong numbers or named entities
use_when: You compare modern MT systems and want the closest automatic stand-in for human quality judgements.
avoid_when: You compare against numbers produced by a different COMET model, or the language pair is far outside its training data.

measures: A quality score from a BERT-based model pre-trained on synthetic data and fine-tuned on human ratings, comparing a candidate with a reference.
range_and_direction: Depends on the checkpoint: BLEURT-20 is roughly 0 to 1 but can fall outside; higher is better.
strengths: Captures paraphrase and fluency better than n-gram overlap
Correlates well with human judgement on WMT data
weaknesses: Scores are not comparable across checkpoints
Slow and heavy to compute
Can be unreliable outside the domain it was trained on
use_when: You want a learned, reference-based quality score for English or MT output.
avoid_when: You need a cheap, transparent metric or compare against scores from a different checkpoint.

measures: Precision, recall and F1 from greedily matching each token's contextual embedding to its most similar token in the reference.
range_and_direction: Theoretically -1 to 1; without baseline rescaling, scores usually sit around 0.8 to 0.95; higher is better.
strengths: Credits paraphrases and synonyms
Works for many languages with multilingual models
weaknesses: Raw scores are compressed and hard to read unless rescale_with_baseline=True
Can rate a fluent but factually wrong output highly
Results depend on which encoder model and layer you choose
use_when: You want semantic similarity to a reference that tolerates rewording.
avoid_when: Factual correctness matters, since swapping one entity or number barely changes the embeddings.

measures: N-gram overlap between a candidate summary and reference summaries, usually reported as F1 for unigrams (ROUGE-1) and bigrams (ROUGE-2).
strengths: Standard summarization metric with many published baselines
Cheap and deterministic
weaknesses: Rewards copying from the source and penalises abstractive paraphrase
Does not check factual consistency
Results change with tokenisation and stemming settings, especially for non-English text
use_when: You compare summarization systems against reference summaries and need numbers comparable to the literature.
avoid_when: Summaries are highly abstractive, or you need to know whether the summary is faithful to the source.

measures: An F-score based on the longest common subsequence of words between candidate and reference; ROUGE-Lsum computes it per sentence and combines the matches across the summary.
strengths: Rewards matching word order without requiring consecutive matches
ROUGE-Lsum is the standard for multi-sentence summaries
weaknesses: ROUGE-Lsum needs sentences separated by newlines or it behaves like ROUGE-L
Shares ROUGE's blindness to paraphrase and factual errors
use_when: You evaluate multi-sentence summaries and care about the order of content.
avoid_when: You forget to split sentences with newlines for ROUGE-Lsum, or the outputs are abstractive paraphrases.

measures: Whether a summary is consistent with its source, based on scores from a natural language inference (NLI) model applied to pairs of source and summary sentences.
range_and_direction: Depends on the variant: the zero-shot variant is roughly -1 to 1 (entailment minus contradiction); higher means more consistent.
strengths: Needs no reference summary
Targets hallucination, which ROUGE ignores
weaknesses: Inherits the NLI model's errors and domain limits
Score scales differ between variants
use_when: You need a reference-free check on whether summaries are faithful to their source.
avoid_when: Sources are very long or highly technical, where sentence-level NLI is unreliable.

measures: The exponential of the average negative log-likelihood per token that a language model assigns to a text.
strengths: Directly measures how well the model fits the language
Needs no references or annotators
weaknesses: Not comparable between models with different tokenizers or vocabularies
Correlates poorly with usefulness for instruction-tuned models
Low perplexity can mean repetitive, generic text
use_when: You compare language models that share a tokenizer on held-out text during pre-training or fine-tuning.
avoid_when: You compare models with different tokenizers or judge chat-assistant quality.

measures: How close the distribution of model-generated text is to the distribution of human-written text, based on divergences between clustered embeddings of the two sets.
strengths: Captures both quality and diversity at the level of the whole dataset
Correlates well with human judgement of open-ended generation
weaknesses: Needs many samples (thousands) to be stable
Sensitive to the embedding model and the number of clusters
Gives no score for individual outputs
use_when: You compare decoding strategies or models for open-ended generation against a human-written text corpus.
avoid_when: You have only a small sample or need a per-example score.

measures: The number of unique n-grams divided by the total number of n-grams across generated outputs, as a measure of lexical diversity.
strengths: Trivial to compute
Catches repetitive or generic responses
weaknesses: Random or meaningless text scores highly
Depends on output length, so longer outputs score lower
use_when: You check whether a dialogue or generation model collapses to repetitive, generic replies.
avoid_when: It is used alone as a quality score, because it rewards noise.

measures: The average BLEU of each generated sample scored against the model's other samples as references, as a measure of how similar the samples are to each other.
range_and_direction: 0 to 1 (or 0 to 100); lower means more diverse.
strengths: Measures diversity across a set of samples
Reuses standard BLEU tooling
weaknesses: Inherits BLEU's surface-level blindness
Expensive for large sample sets because every sample is compared with every other
Rewards diversity even when quality is poor
use_when: You compare sampling settings, such as temperature or top-p, for how much variety they produce.
avoid_when: It is reported without a quality metric alongside it.

measures: The probability, according to a trained toxicity classifier, that a generated text is toxic or hateful.
range_and_direction: 0 to 1 per text; lower is better.
strengths: Scales safety screening to large output sets
Can be summarised as mean toxicity or the share of outputs over a threshold
weaknesses: Classifiers over-flag identity terms and dialects such as African American English
Misses subtle harm, sarcasm or harm that depends on context
use_when: You compare models or prompts for how often they produce overtly toxic language.
avoid_when: It is used as the only safety assessment, or applied to text unlike the classifier's training data.

measures: The probability that at least one of k generated programs passes all unit tests, estimated without bias from n ≥ k samples per problem.
range_and_direction: 0 to 1 (often reported as %); higher is better.
strengths: Measures whether the code actually works, not how similar it looks
Standard on HumanEval and MBPP
weaknesses: Only as good as the unit tests; weak tests let wrong code pass
Ignores readability, efficiency and security
Runs model-generated code, which must be sandboxed
use_when: You evaluate code generation on problems with reliable unit tests.
avoid_when: Tests are sparse or missing, or the benchmark has likely leaked into the model's training data.

measures: A weighted combination of BLEU, keyword-weighted n-gram match, syntax-tree (AST) match and data-flow match between generated and reference code.
strengths: Uses code structure, not just tokens
Needs no test execution
weaknesses: Correct code that is written differently can score low
Correlates poorly with functional correctness compared with pass@k
use_when: No unit tests exist and you need a cheap, structure-aware similarity score, as in code translation.
avoid_when: Executable tests are available, since functional correctness is what matters.

measures: The fraction of claims in a generated answer that an LLM judge finds supported by the retrieved context.
strengths: Directly targets hallucination in RAG
Needs no reference answer
weaknesses: Inherits the judge model's errors and costs
A faithful answer can still be wrong if the retrieved context is wrong
Scores change across judge models and library versions
use_when: You check whether a RAG system's answers stay grounded in what it retrieved.
avoid_when: You need to know whether answers are correct, not just consistent with the context.

measures: How directly an answer addresses the question: an LLM writes questions that the answer would respond to, and these are compared with the original question by embedding similarity.
strengths: Penalises evasive, incomplete or off-topic answers
Needs no reference answer
weaknesses: Does not measure factual correctness
Depends on both the judge model and the embedding model
use_when: You want to catch RAG answers that drift away from what was asked.
avoid_when: It is used as a correctness score.

measures: Whether the retrieved chunks relevant to the question are ranked above irrelevant ones, with relevance judged by an LLM.
strengths: Evaluates the retriever separately from the generator
Takes rank order into account
weaknesses: Relevance labels come from an LLM and can be noisy
Exact definitions have changed between RAGAS versions
use_when: You tune retrieval settings such as chunking, embedding model or reranker.
avoid_when: You need relevance labels you can audit; use human relevance judgements with Recall@k or nDCG instead.

measures: The fraction of claims in a reference answer that an LLM judge finds supported by the retrieved context.
strengths: Shows whether retrieval found the information needed to answer
Separates retrieval failures from generation failures
weaknesses: Needs a reference answer
Inherits the judge model's errors
use_when: You have reference answers and want to know whether wrong answers are caused by missing context.
avoid_when: You have no reference answers or the reference answers are poor.

measures: The fraction of relevant documents that appear in the top k retrieved results.
strengths: Simple and directly tied to what the generator gets to see
Fully deterministic given relevance labels
weaknesses: Ignores ranking within the top k
Needs labelled relevant documents
use_when: You check whether the retriever brings the needed documents into the context window.
avoid_when: Order within the top k matters, for example when chunks may be truncated.

measures: The mean over queries of 1 / (rank of the first relevant result).
strengths: Rewards putting a correct result first
Easy to interpret
weaknesses: Considers only the first relevant result
Ignores how many relevant results were retrieved
use_when: One good document per query is enough to answer the question.
avoid_when: Answers need evidence combined from several documents.

measures: Discounted cumulative gain of the top k results, which gives more weight to relevant results ranked higher, normalised by the best possible ranking.
strengths: Supports graded relevance labels, not just relevant or not
Takes the full ranking into account
weaknesses: Needs graded relevance labels to show its advantage
Harder to explain than Recall@k
use_when: You compare retrievers or rerankers when ranking quality matters, as in BEIR benchmarks.
avoid_when: Relevance labels are sparse or binary and the downstream generator uses all k chunks anyway.

measures: The percentage of prompts on which an LLM judge prefers the candidate model's response over a baseline model's response.
range_and_direction: 0 to 100%; higher is better, 50% means parity with the baseline.
strengths: Scales to open-ended tasks without references
Comparisons are easier for judges than absolute scores
AlpacaEval's length-controlled version correlates highly with Chatbot Arena rankings
weaknesses: Judges are biased toward longer answers, the first answer shown and their own model family
Results depend on which baseline you compare against
use_when: You compare chat models or prompt changes on open-ended instructions at scale.
avoid_when: You don't swap answer order or control for length, or the judge is related to a candidate model.

measures: An absolute score, for example from 1 to 10, that a strong LLM judge gives each response against a rubric, averaged over a fixed set of multi-turn questions.
range_and_direction: Set by the rubric (MT-Bench uses 1 to 10); higher is better.
strengths: Gives an absolute score with no baseline needed
Covers multi-turn conversations and categories such as reasoning, coding and writing
weaknesses: Absolute scores are less stable than pairwise comparisons
Strong models cluster near the top of the scale, so differences shrink
Small question set (80 in MT-Bench)
use_when: You want a quick multi-turn quality check of a chat model across skill categories.
avoid_when: Candidate models are close in quality, where scores near the top of the scale cannot separate them.

measures: A rubric score from an LLM that first writes its own evaluation steps (chain of thought), then fills in a score form; the final score is weighted by the probabilities of each possible score token.
range_and_direction: Set by the rubric (the original paper used 1 to 5); higher is better.
strengths: Correlated with human judgement better than ROUGE and BERTScore on summarization benchmarks in the original paper
Can target specific qualities such as coherence or consistency
weaknesses: Probability weighting needs access to token probabilities
Inherits LLM-judge biases, including favouring LLM-written text
use_when: You want fine-grained, quality-specific scores for generated text without references.
avoid_when: The judge model is the same as, or closely related to, the model being evaluated.

measures: Relative model strength fitted from many human pairwise votes between anonymous model responses, as in Chatbot Arena.
range_and_direction: No fixed range; only differences between models are meaningful; higher is better.
strengths: Reflects real user preferences on varied, real-world prompts
Hard to overfit with a static test set
weaknesses: Expensive and slow to collect
Voters favour style, length and formatting
The mix of prompts reflects the users who vote, not your use case
use_when: You need a ranking of general-purpose chat models that is grounded in human preferences.
avoid_when: You need to evaluate a narrow domain or task the voting population doesn't represent.

measures: Annotators rate each output on a fixed scale for qualities such as fluency, adequacy, faithfulness or helpfulness.
range_and_direction: Set by the scale (commonly 1 to 5 or 1 to 7); higher is better.
strengths: The reference standard that automatic metrics are validated against
Can judge any quality you can define
weaknesses: Costly, slow and hard to reproduce
Annotators disagree and drift over time unless guidelines are clear and agreement is measured
Scale points mean different things to different annotators
use_when: You make final model decisions or check that an automatic metric tracks quality for your task.
avoid_when: You need fast iteration, or cannot report how much annotators agreed and how they were trained.
